episode_title: MORE Stories That Should be Films

stories.summary: Inspired by a strange dream the show's cinematographer Vaishnav had about Ajay, Amit spins a fully-storyboarded film about a geeky, unmarried man in his fifties living in a shabby Bandra-East-style flat who walks the building every morning collecting all the residents' electricity bills. He runs a quiet racket with a friend in the electricity department: cut the supply of those who haven't paid, then 'Ajaybhai' graciously gets it reconnected for a bill amount, late fee, and bribe, splitting the proceeds. A frail older woman moves in alone; her bill gets stolen, she's too ill to chase it; he visits, is moved, makes (well, jugaads) dal-chawal for her, and a tentative love begins. She's obsessive-compulsive; she discovers his stash of stolen bills in his bathroom cupboard while trying to shut a door that springs back, and storms out. After a tense night where he expects the police, she chooses not to report him; he reforms, and the closing shot is split-screen — every door in the building opening to find the bill restored, possibly breaking into a Bollywood-style song over the credits.
stories.insight: A character study of a small-time rent-seeker as a sympathetic, lonely human — the same model of the Indian state's hafta-and-reconnection culture, but with the geek-hoarder's compulsion as the engine. The real lesson is in the craft: invoke Chekhov's gun, show-don't-tell, plant the wires, the Maggi packets, the OCD prep board — every prop must fire later.

stories.topic: The Khalsa Bridge — Bota Singh and Garja Singh, 1739
stories.summary: Drawn from Sarpreet Singh's 'The Rise of the Sikhs.' In a Punjab dominated by the Mughal subedar Zakaria Khan, two young Sikh fighters, Bota Singh and Garja Singh (also called Mota), are hiding in fields when a farmer scoffs that they're not lions but jackals — real Singhs would fight, not hide. Stung, they 'conquer' an empty wooden bridge near Sarai Nurdin and impose a 'Khalsa regime tax' — one paisa per donkey, six paisas per cart. Astonishingly, travellers just pay. They get rich but feel hollow — they wanted glory, not commerce. Bota then writes a taunting letter to Zakaria Khan, addressing him as 'sister-in-law,' demanding he respond. A bored Zakaria Khan sends a hundred horses; the two Sikhs fight wave after wave, are eventually shot in the legs, and in the climactic 'one-legged last stand,' they wrap their arms around each other, stand on their one remaining functional leg back-to-back, and die fighting.
stories.insight: A meditation on alienation and the search for meaning: men dying in futile battles to prove things — to others, to themselves. Amit asks whether all of us, in our smaller ways, aren't just Bota Singh and Garja Singh standing on one leg against the power of bad ideas. Also a rare case where history survives only from the loser's side — a Rajinikanth-style retelling preserved by Sikh chroniclers, not the victorious Mughals.

stories.topic: Two Chess Stories — Sultan Khan and Mr. B
stories.summary: Amit weaves Stefan Zweig's novella 'The Royal Game' (a.k.a. 'Chess Story') together with the real life of Sultan Khan. Zweig's Mr. B, a Nazi prisoner with only a chess book in solitary confinement, memorises games and creates an alter ego to play against — emerging as a peerless tactical calculator. Sultan Khan, born 1903 in a family of mirs and landlords, taught himself chess, won the British Chess Championship in 1928 and twice more, then returned to India at 34 and never played again. Amit fictionalises Sultan as a 'black sheep's son' whose victories restore his father's, family's, and nation's pride — an intuitive, positional player who 'sees' endgame pawn structures from move eight, the polar opposite of Mr. B's brute calculation. In the climactic fictional game, Sultan deliberately throws the match, recognising that the real game he has been playing all his life — for respect — was never the game on the board.
stories.insight: Chess as an instrument of self-actualisation: two utterly different inner lives — one trapped in solitude, one trapped in expectation — meet across the board. Two masteries arrived at by entirely different paths (deep tactical calculation vs intuitive positional sense), echoing Adriaan de Groot's finding that grandmasters and novices look ahead the same number of moves; what differs is pattern recognition. The deeper twist: the most meaningful move in a chess life can be choosing to lose.

stories.topic: The Postal Boy — children mailed through the US Postal System
stories.summary: In 19th-century America, the post office created the public good of universal parcel delivery — drop off potatoes, wheat, anything, get it routed across the country at modest prices. One day, half as a joke, parents asked to post their child; the postal employees weighed him, calculated correct charges, pasted the destination address on his shirt, and routed him through sorting centres exactly like a parcel. It worked. It became a thing. For years, American parents posted their kids — unaccompanied, unescorted — and post-office employees fed and forwarded them along. Amit improvises a sub-plot: a drunk dad takes a bet to post his surly, unloved son; a storm strands the boy in a sorting depot; an older postman whose own children have abandoned him forms a quiet bond with the parcel before sending him on.
stories.insight: A staggering snapshot of trust capital — parents, postal workers, and children all comfortable trusting strangers' good behaviour across an entire continent. Ajay's 'rules of the situation' approach to film: set up an absurd-but-real institutional premise, leave the human drama to the storyteller. Reality is stranger than fiction, and the ordinariness with which Americans turned children into legal parcels says more about social capital than any survey could.

recommendations.creator: Samuel Beckett
recommendations.context: The play whose alienated tramps Vladimir and Estragon Amit invokes as a model for how to write Bota Singh and Garja Singh.
recommendations.reason: Two characters waiting for nothing, riffing on each other, embody the kind of tragicomic alienation Amit wants for his Khalsa-bridge film.

recommendations.creator: Tom Stoppard
recommendations.context: Stoppard's play that takes two minor friends of Hamlet and centres them.
recommendations.reason: Another model for writing two seemingly minor figures into the moral centre of a story — useful template for Bota and Garja's interior life.

recommendations.creator: Sarpreet Singh
recommendations.context: The book in which Amit found the Bota Singh and Garja Singh story, including Sarpreet's English translation of Bota Singh's taunting Punjabi letter to Zakaria Khan.
recommendations.reason: Magnificent history, source for the Khalsa-bridge episode; Sarpreet has also recorded with Amit on The Seen and the Unseen.

recommendations.item: The Royal Game (also published as Chess Story)
recommendations.creator: Stefan Zweig
recommendations.context: Zweig's novella about a chess world champion challenged on a ship by a mysterious Mr. B who learnt the game in Nazi solitary confinement.
recommendations.reason: A deeply moving story of chess as the only company in solitude — Amit had recommended it on the show before; Zweig committed suicide a year after its release.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's old ESPN piece on Anand, in which he likens Anand's self-taught journey to 'taking a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race' against the systematically-trained Soviet school.
recommendations.reason: The piece anticipates the Sultan-Khan parallel — Indian players rising through intuition rather than osmosis.

recommendations.creator: Adriaan de Groot
recommendations.context: The mid-twentieth-century study comparing how many moves ahead grandmasters versus novices think.
recommendations.reason: The famous result: they look the same number of moves ahead — what separates them is pattern recognition. Sets up Amit's contrast between Mr. B's calculation and Sultan Khan's positional sense.

core_ideas.explanation: Anton Chekhov's principle that if you show a gun in the first act, it must go off by the third — nothing in a story should be there for no reason. Amit applies this to filmic show-don't-tell: every prop in the bachelor's flat (the wires, the Maggi packets, the dip-dip tea, the OCD chopping board) is planted so it can fire later in the plot — the geek hoarding sets up the bill-collecting compulsion; the bad cooking sets up the failed dal-chawal; the OCD sets up her trying to shut the cupboard.
core_ideas.quote: If you show a gun in the first act of the play, it must go off by the third.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's central craft principle: never spell out motivation, sociology, or backstory; reveal them through props, gestures, and choices. He explicitly contrasts this with mainstream films that 'try to locate the why' — when Ajay suggests anchoring the story in a Marxist concept of alienation, Amit says alienation should be felt, not announced. 'All the bate happens to Nasro' — all the telling is absent, it's all showing.
core_ideas.quote: All the bate happens to Nasro. All the telling is absent. It's all showing.

core_ideas.concept: The Rent-Seeker as Human, the State as Scam
core_ideas.explanation: The Collector of Bills is a one-man dramatisation of the Indian state — a small operator who creates an artificial scarcity (a missing bill), then heroically resolves it, taking 'a bill amount, a late fee, a bribe' and splitting the proceeds with his accomplice in the electricity department. Bota and Garja, charging an unauthorised toll on a bridge they 'conquered,' are forced to confront whether they're traders or rent-seekers. Bota's verdict: 'we are like crooks or government' — to him, synonyms.
core_ideas.quote: We are like crooks or government — which to him are synonyms. And in most contexts they are.

core_ideas.concept: Alienation and the Battle for Respect
core_ideas.explanation: The thread linking three of the four stories. Bota and Garja fight a futile war to gain respect — from the farmer who called them jackals, from each other, from themselves. Sultan Khan is forced into chess as a 'battle for respect' — for himself, his father (the family's black sheep), his family, his nation. The bill collector is alienated in his messy bachelor pad until a frail neighbour gives him a reason to cook. The deeper question Amit keeps returning to: 'Is everything is everything a futile battle?'
core_ideas.quote: How many lives are lost because you are anxious to prove things to others, because you are anxious to prove things to yourself.

core_ideas.concept: History Told Only From the Loser's Side
core_ideas.explanation: History is normally written by winners, but the Bota Singh / Garja Singh tale survives only in Sikh retellings — the Mughals' victorious account is silent. The result is a 'Rajinikanth' retelling: two men repelling waves of a hundred horses, one shooting them in the legs, then a one-legged last stand where they wrap arms around each other and die fighting. A curious inversion of the usual archive bias.

core_ideas.concept: Two Roads to Mastery — Calculation vs Pattern
core_ideas.explanation: Mr. B masters chess in solitary confinement through brute calculation — playing himself thousands of times, his lines reach engine-like depth. Sultan Khan, never having read a chess book or talked chess with anyone, masters it through positional intuition — sensing on move eight what the endgame pawn structure will be. Adriaan de Groot's study: grandmasters and novices think the same number of moves ahead; what separates them is pattern recognition. Two utterly different paths to the same summit.

Ajay's frame for the postal-boy story. A society's willingness to trust strangers — parents trusting postal workers with their child, postal workers feeding and routing kids, the kids themselves comfortable with the journey — is a kind of capital that enables institutions to do absurd, generous things. The fact that Americans posted children for years says more about social trust than any explicit survey could. The implicit contrast with modern India: would you mail your child today?

core_ideas.concept: Two Models of Filmmaking — Animator vs Architect
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay defines the difference openly: his concept of 'stories that should be films' is to set up the rules of a situation and 'leave the human drama as an exercise to the reader,' requiring 'a genius like you to animate it with people and desires.' Amit, by contrast, builds the entire interior life — backstories, motivations, prop placements, the close-up of a delicate wrist on a fork — and gives the institutional setting only as much weight as the camera needs.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit announces 'Amit Varma is gonna tell you stories. Great Amit Varma and the even greater Ajay Shah are going to tell you stories.'
On why he didn't cast Vaishnav as Ajay's film alter ego: 'I said you're too young and handsome — which is not to say you are not handsome, but you are not young.'
On the OCD cupboard door that won't stay shut: 'It springs back out like an adamant economist. She pushes it in. It springs back out further like a non-recalcitrant communist.'

Amit on the doomed line every man has used: 'Have you ever been in a fight with a woman, Ajay-sha, where you have said something like I can explain, knowing that you can't?' — followed by addressing 'gentle male readers, in this time I specify gentle male readers.'
Crew suggestion: Vaishnav and Namita keep telling Ajay he'd be a perfect fit for Walter White from Breaking Bad.

Amit's confession of his one-grandmaster boast: he beat Abhijit Kunte in a Blitz game with a queen sacrifice — what he doesn't mention is that he was 17, Kunte was 14 and not yet a grandmaster, and across dozens of other Blitz games Kunte surely beat him every time. Ajay's reply: 'It is sweet joy to win even once.'

Bota Singh's calculated insult in his letter to Zakaria Khan — addressing the Mughal governor as 'my sister-in-law, my dear Khan.' Amit: 'In his mind, every man-day man is an emperor, Ajay-sha, isn't it? Right? Except you. So you are the economist.'

Why bored emperors start wars: 'Number one, there are no ongoing wars. Number two, there is no television, no internet, no mobile phone, no OTTs to watch. So Zakaria Khan is bored. And he says, fuck it. I'm gonna go.'

Ajay's modern-day postal-boy parallel: a friend in Bangalore who couldn't get an Uber 'dunzos himself' — calls Dunzo, books a parcel delivery from office to home, and rides on the back of the scooter.
Amit's pitch for the closing credits song over the bill-restoration finale: take any Hindi song and 'do a Dil-Bil swap' — 'Bil Hi Toh Hai' — to score the dancing residents.

Walter White (Breaking Bad) — invoked because a 'pivotal moment of reveal' in that show happens in a toilet, mirroring the bathroom scene in which the OCD neighbour discovers the cupboard of stolen bills.
Alpha Zero — invoked as the modern echo of Mr. B's chess-against-himself in Zweig's Royal Game; the prisoner trains by self-play 'in the glorious tradition of Alpha Zero.'
Ahimsa, traders not raiders — Amit calls back to an earlier EIE episode on the Indian preference for trade over plunder when Garja Singh wonders aloud whether they should just stay traders.
Indians eventually barred from the British Chess Championship after RB Ramesh and Abhijit Kunte won in the early 2000s — 'fuck it, these Indians are winning it, no more Indians.'
Fischer-Spassky, Gukesh — Ajay name-checks the great chess matches with a strong psychological aspect, the kind that 'stick out' in memory.
